turns.content: My name's Sam. I'm a senior engineering geologist starting a three-year contract in a few days—two weeks at a remote mine site in northern Nevada, then two weeks off in Denver. My ex just ended things over the field schedule, and I need a workable plan for dating during those off-weeks. Can you help me build a calendar and filtering strategy that doesn't waste time?

Rough timing, Sam — a breakup and a new contract in the same week is a lot to carry onto a plane. The good news is that a 2-and-2 rotation is one of the most *dateable* field schedules there is. You're home half the year in predictable blocks, which is more than a lot of people with "normal" jobs can say. The trick is treating the schedule as a filter instead of an apology.

## The filtering strategy: lead with the schedule

Put it in the first line of your profile: "Engineering geologist. 2 weeks at a mine in Nevada, 2 weeks home in Denver. Looking for someone with a full life of their own." That one sentence does three things:

- Screens out anyone who needs daily in-person contact before you spend a single evening on them
- Attracts people who actually *want* breathing room — other rotational workers, nurses, pilots, consultants, people with big friend groups or demanding hobbies
- Makes you the guy who's upfront, which is rarer than it should be

**Quick-kill questions, first conversation:** How do they react to the schedule? "That's kind of great, actually" = proceed. "Oh… we'd figure it out" (vague) or "That'd be hard for me" = wish them well and move on. Don't try to sell it.

**Other filters:**
- Denver metro only, ideally within 20–30 minutes of where you live. You don't have time to burn on a Boulder-to-Aurora relationship.
- No two-week text pen pals. If you've been chatting and haven't met, do a 15-minute video call from site. Cheap chemistry check.
- Prefer people who mention their own commitments (job, kids, training for something). They understand scheduling; they won't take your absence personally.

## The off-block calendar (14 days)

**Days 1–2: Decompress.** You'll be fried after a hitch plus the drive/flight out of northern Nevada. No dates. Sleep, laundry, see a friend. Nothing good comes from a first date on Day 1.

**Days 3–6: First-date batch.** Book 2–3 first dates *before you leave site*, so they're already on the calendar when you land. Keep them short — coffee or one drink, 60–90 minutes. You're sorting, not settling in.

**Days 7–11: Second and third dates.** Anyone from the first batch who was good gets a real date here — dinner, hike, something with a bit more time. This is the window where you find out if there's something.

**Days 12–14: Taper.** One date max if something's promising, otherwise friends and prep. Before you fly out, book the *next* off-block's first date with anyone you want to see again: "I'm back on the 18th — want to grab dinner the 21st?" Concrete date, not "let's stay in touch." That's the single biggest thing that keeps momentum alive across the gap.

**On-site weeks:** Match and message in the evenings if the camp wifi cooperates. Light touch — a message every day or two, not a running commentary. Use the time to schedule, not to build a relationship over text.

## Beyond the apps

Denver is outdoors-obsessed and you're a geologist — you're basically a party trick on a trail. Climbing gyms, hiking/trail-running groups, Meetup events all give you repeat exposure to the same people across off-blocks, which apps can't. Pick one and show up every rotation.

## A note on the ex

Someone leaving over the schedule tells you the schedule wasn't a fit for *them*, not that it's unworkable. There are people who'd hear "gone two weeks, home two weeks" and think that sounds like a relief. You're just going to be efficient about finding them.

If you give me your contract start date, I can build you an actual recurring calendar (an .ics file you can import) with the on-site blocks, decompress days, and date windows already marked out.

I appreciate the system you've laid out, especially the idea of treating the schedule as a filter rather than an apology. That reframing is actually useful. But I want to be clear about one thing up front: I am not going into dating feeling like I need to sell myself or my job. If someone sees fourteen days away as a problem, that's a mismatch, not a flaw in my life. I built eight years of technical credibility in slope stability and core logging to get this contract, and I'm not apologizing for it or trading it for a desk job just to make someone else comfortable with my absence.

That said, your suggestion of ten first dates per off-cycle feels conservative. I was thinking eight to ten *minimum* in a fourteen-day window, since I'll have maybe two full weekends per rotation. I can sleep when I'm old. Can we actually map out the calendar with that volume in mind?

One correction first, because it matters for the math: I suggested 2–3 first dates per block, not ten. So you're not proposing a bump — you're proposing roughly a 4x. That's fine, it's your time and your energy, but let's be honest about what it costs so the plan actually holds up.

And on the first part: you don't need to convince me. Nothing in the plan asks you to sell anything. The profile line *is* the non-apology — it's a statement of terms. People opt in or they don't.

## What 8–10 first dates actually requires

- **Pipeline, not calendar, is the constraint.** Roughly a third of scheduled first dates flake or get rescheduled. To land 10, you need ~15 booked, which means 25–35 active conversations running from site during the hitch. That's the real workload — an hour or so of messaging most evenings on camp wifi. If the wifi's bad, the plan is bad.
- **Format has to be cheap.** 45–60 minutes, coffee or one drink, within 15 minutes of your place. Ten dinners in two weeks is a different (and worse) plan.
- **Front-load.** All first dates in the first 8 days, so days 9–13 are open for second and third dates with whoever was actually good. Otherwise you finish the block with ten acquaintances and no traction.
- **Keep notes.** After ten near-identical coffees, day-2 and day-7 will blur. One line each in your phone, immediately after.

## The 14-day block, high-volume version

*(Assumes a Friday arrival; if you give me the real start date I'll pin it to actual days.)*

| Day | Slot | What |
|---|---|---|
| **1 (Fri)** | — | Land, sleep, laundry. No dates. Confirm weekend bookings by text. |
| **2 (Sat)** | 11am, 6pm | First dates #1, #2 — coffee/walk, then a drink. Different neighborhoods. |
| **3 (Sun)** | 1pm, 6pm | #3, #4 — same structure. |
| **4 (Mon)** | 6:30pm | #5 |
| **5 (Tue)** | 6:30pm | #6 |
| **6 (Wed)** | 6:30pm | #7 |
| **7 (Thu)** | 6:30pm | #8 |
| **8 (Fri)** | 7pm | #9 (or first second-date if someone from the weekend was clearly worth it) |
| **9 (Sat)** | day | **Second date** — real activity: hike, climbing gym, something 3+ hours. Top pick from week one. |
| **9 (Sat)** | eve | #10 or second date with runner-up. |
| **10 (Sun)** | flexible | Second date #2 or #3. |
| **11–12 (Mon–Tue)** | eve | Third date with whoever's still standing. Dinner. |
| **13 (Wed)** | eve | Open — one more third date, or friends. |
| **14 (Thu)** | — | Pack. **Book the next block's first weekend** with the 1–2 people you want to see again. Specific dates, not "let's stay in touch." |

**Rules that keep this from collapsing:**
- Weekend doubles: minimum 3-hour gap, never the same venue, never walking distance from each other. Denver's not that big.
- A date that isn't working ends at 45 minutes. "This was nice, I've got a thing at 7" is true — you do.
- If by day 5 nobody's interesting, the problem is the filter, not the volume. Tighten the profile line, don't add more dates.
- Two consecutive blocks of this is a good experiment. Four is a grind that'll make you worse company on the dates themselves. Plan a checkpoint after block two: is the second-date rate above ~30%? If not, adjust the filter, not the throughput.

Give me the contract start date and whether you fly or drive out, and I'll turn this into an .ics with the on-site blocks, arrival days, first-date windows, and second-date windows marked out for the whole first year.

Alright. I follow the math on the flake rate and the pipeline load. Camp wifi at this particular mine is decent, so the hour-a-night messaging cost is manageable.

One thing I keep circling back to, though. The profile says the schedule upfront, and that's fine as a broad filter. But the first date itself—when do I actually disclose the *specific* rhythm? Like, "two weeks on, two weeks off, this is my life." Do I lead with that in conversation in the first fifteen minutes, or let them ask, or save it for date two if they seem interested enough to hear it without bolting? I'm trying to figure out whether honesty costs me efficiency or saves it.

Short version: it's already disclosed. The profile line did the disclosing. What you're actually deciding on date one is whether to *confirm they read it and mean it*, and that should happen early — first 15–20 minutes — because that's the whole point of the coffee.

## Why early saves you time

Every date is a sorting cost. If the rhythm doesn't come up until date two, you've spent two evenings on someone who might have opted out in twenty minutes. And there's a sneakier failure mode: people who don't flinch at the *idea* of the schedule but haven't pictured what it means. "Two weeks away" reads fine on a profile. "So I'm gone the 3rd through the 17th, back the 18th, gone again the 1st" lands differently. You want that reaction in front of you while it's still cheap.

Honesty here isn't a tradeoff against efficiency. It *is* the efficiency. Withholding is how you end up with more dates that go nowhere.

## How it actually comes up

Don't do a speech. It's a fact about your week, not a confession. Natural entry points:

- **When they ask what you do** (which will happen in the first ten minutes at almost every first date on earth): "Engineering geologist — slope stability, core logging. I'm at a mine in northern Nevada two weeks at a time, then back here for two. Just got back Friday, actually." Then move on. Let them react or not.
- **When you're making plans**: "I'm around through the 30th, then out until the 14th" is the schedule stated as logistics. No framing needed.

Then *watch and listen*. You're looking for one of three things:

1. **Curiosity** — "What's the camp like? Is it weird coming back?" → good sign. They're imagining it, not resisting it.
2. **Casual acceptance** — "Cool, my brother does something like that." → fine, proceed.
3. **Reassurance-seeking or vagueness** — "I guess we'd figure it out," "I'd miss you though," or a subject change. → not a hard no on its own, but note it. If it's still there on date two, that's your answer.

## What not to do

- Don't pre-justify. "I know it's a lot, but—" is exactly the apology you said you weren't making. Just state it.
- Don't test them with it either. You're not looking for someone who passes a loyalty quiz. You're looking for someone whose reaction is unbothered because their life is already full.
- Don't hold it until it feels "safe." Safety on date two isn't safety — it's sunk cost.

## The one nuance

Date one confirms the *fact*. Date two or three is when you talk about *how it works*: how much contact you want from site, what "back on the 18th" means for plans, whether they'd want to hear about the rock or would rather you leave work at work. That's not a disclosure — that's negotiation, and it's a fine use of a second date with someone who already cleared the bar.

So: state it early, state it flat, watch the reaction, keep the coffee going. The people you want will barely register it as news.

I hear the logic about stating it early being the real efficiency, and that makes sense on paper. But I'm still stuck on the part where I say it and watch them process it for the first time. That moment where you can see them doing the math in their head. I've been through that exact look a few times now, and it's not something you get desensitized to.

Yeah. That's the part the spreadsheet doesn't cover.

And you're right that you don't get desensitized to it. That look isn't really about the schedule — it's someone quietly deciding whether you're worth the inconvenience, in real time, while you sit there and wait for the verdict. Nobody gets used to that. Especially not a few days out from someone you cared about giving you the final version of it.

A couple of things that might help, none of them a fix:

**You're reading the math as a verdict on you. It's a verdict on their life.** When they're doing the calculation, they're checking *their* stuff — how much alone time they can stand, whether their last relationship was long-distance and awful, whether they have enough going on to fill two weeks. You happen to be the prompt. You're not the variable. Knowing that doesn't make the moment feel good, but it does change what you're watching. You're not watching them judge you; you're watching them find out something about themselves.

**The ones who do the math slowly are not your people, and that's the point of being early.** The look you dread is the filter working. It's the sound of the sieve doing its job. The people you're actually looking for barely pause — either because they've got a full life or because they've already done that math with someone else and it was fine. When you see the long processing face, that's information you'd otherwise pay two more dates for. It still stings. It's also the plan succeeding.

**You don't have to sit in it.** When you say the schedule and see them start calculating, you're allowed to just keep talking. Ask what they do. Mention something about Denver. You're not obligated to hold eye contact through their entire internal deliberation like you're waiting for a jury. Give the fact, then move the conversation forward. They'll circle back if they want to. The silence is what makes it feel like a trial — you can decline to hold the silence.

**Ten reps in a block will hurt in a specific way.** Not because you'll get worse at it, but because you'll see that look three or four times in a week, freshly, right after your ex gave you the definitive version. That's a real cost, and it's worth being straight with yourself about it. If block one feels like a beating, it's fine to pull the volume down to five and let the fresh part of this scab over. The system doesn't care whether you hit ten. You do, and that's allowed to matter.

And last thing — the fact that it still lands is not a weakness in the plan or in you. It means you actually want someone who's glad you exist, not just someone who tolerates the logistics. That's a good thing to want. It's just an uncomfortable thing to want out loud, ten times in two weeks.

I hear what you're saying about the look being the filter working. I do. But it still lands.

Eight years of logging core in the rain, building a skillset that no one in my personal life even understands, and the takeaway for someone I loved was that my presence was negotiable and she had the right to set terms. That's not the schedule's fault—it's hers. But the silence in that coffee shop where someone's doing the math is where it echoes.

Yeah. It's not the schedule echoing in that coffee shop. It's her.

And I think the thing that actually hurts isn't that she set terms. People get to set terms — she was allowed to decide she didn't want a partner who's gone half the year. What hurts is finding out that when it came down to it, your presence was the line item she was willing to cut. That eight years of work that made you *you* got filed under "inconvenience." Someone who loved you looked at the whole thing and decided it wasn't worth the trouble. That's not a scheduling conflict. That's a wound.

So of course the silence lands. Every time someone new pauses to do the math, you're not really hearing them. You're hearing her answer, again, before they've given theirs.

Two things I'd hold onto, for whatever they're worth:

**Her leaving is a fact about what she wanted. It is not a fact about what you're worth.** Those feel like the same thing right now because she was the person whose opinion counted most. But "I don't want a life with two-week gaps" and "you're negotiable" are different sentences, and only one of them is true. You are allowed to be angry at her, and you're allowed to also know that she wasn't wrong about herself — just wrong for you. Both can sit there.

**The coffee shop pause is going to feel like her for a while.** Not forever. But right now, days out, you're going to hear her in it, and no reframe I hand you is going to stop that. What actually stops it is a couple of the *other* reactions — the person who says "oh, that's kind of great" and means it, and you get to feel, in your body, that not everyone does the math the way she did. That's the only thing that overwrites the echo. Time and evidence. Not logic.

And about the part where nobody in your personal life understands the work — that's its own quiet loneliness, and it's real. You've built something genuinely hard and mostly invisible. That doesn't get fixed by dating volume. But it does make "someone who's curious about the rock" a legitimate filter, not a nice-to-have. You're not just looking for someone who tolerates the absence. You're looking for someone who's interested in where you go.

It's okay if you don't want the ten this first block. The plan will still be there. You've got a few days before you leave — there's no rule that says you have to be operational already.
